title: NASA's Asteroid Crash Test, Up Close: ESA's Hera Reveals a Stadium-Sized Crater on Dimorphos
excerpt: Four years after NASA smashed a spacecraft into an asteroid, ESA's Hera spacecraft has released the first close-up images — revealing a stadium-sized crater...
content:
Four years after NASA deliberately smashed a spacecraft into an asteroid to see whether humanity could nudge a space rock off course, we can finally see what the crash did — and the damage is far bigger than scientists expected.

On November 25, 2026, the European Space Agency released the first close-up images of Dimorphos since the historic collision, taken by its Hera spacecraft. They reveal a stadium-sized crater that stretches across virtually the entire width of the asteroid's impacted face, flattening one side of the rock and leaving strange structures inside it, including what appears to be a cigar-shaped mound at its center.

Dimorphos is a 151-meter-wide asteroid that orbits a much larger space rock, the 730-meter-wide Didymos. On September 26, 2022, NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test — DART — a spacecraft roughly the size of a vending machine, struck Dimorphos at about 22,500 kilometers per hour (14,000 mph) and succeeded in knocking it slightly off course. In October 2024, ESA launched Hera to investigate the aftermath.

Dimorphos is what scientists call a rubble-pile asteroid — a loose collection of rocks held together by gravity rather than a single solid body — and Hera's photographs show something in between solid and rubble. The collision also changed the way Dimorphos rotates: like Earth's Moon, it had been tidally locked to Didymos, always showing the same face.

Perhaps the most unexpected discovery is not on either asteroid, but in the space around them. By combining 11 long-exposure photographs, scientists identified hundreds of boulders orbiting nearby, ranging in size from soccer balls to washing machines. The DART impact is the obvious suspect for the swarm: in 2023, the Hubble Space Telescope identified 37 boulders apparently dislodged by the collision.

Hera will measure Dimorphos's mass and, in January 2027, deploy two shoebox-sized satellites. One, Juventas, will use radar to investigate an asteroid's interior for the first time. The other, Milani, will examine its composition and surrounding dust. NASA plans to launch its dedicated asteroid-hunting telescope, NEO Surveyor, in 2027.

Sources: European Space Agency, Nov. 25, 2026; NASA; ZME Science, Nov. 27, 2026.
